title: TB1-14364
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of China, is seeking refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The claimant's fears emanate from his Falun Gong activities in China. In October 2009, due to the ill health of the claimant's mother, a friend suggested that she practice Falun Gong. Although the claimant and his father were aware of the illegality of this practice, they supported the claimant's mother, but the claimant reminded her to be cautious.

The claimant's mother, after three months, told the claimant how Falun Gong could not only improve their health, but would also cultivate their minds as well. However, he was not interested, but concerned for her safety, he decided to distribute the pamphlets on her behalf beginning in early 2010.

On XXXX XXXX, 2011, the claimant, along with others, were discovered by the patrol police while distributing leaflets. Two members were arrested, however the claimant was able to escape. He hid at the home of a cousin.

On XXXX XXXX, 2011, the Public Security Bureau (PSB) attended the claimant's home. They searched the home but found nothing. His father was questioned about his whereabouts. On the following day, the PSB returned and left a summons for the arrest of the claimant and his mother. As a result, they began to look for a smuggler's assistance.

Following his departure, his mother was allegedly arrested on XXXX XXXX, 2012. The claimant arrived in Canada on August 20, 2011, entering Vancouver illegally, and he filed a refugee claim on August 23, 2011 in Toronto.
The Board finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
The claimant's identity has been established as per the certified true copy of his passport, etc.1 TESTIMONY OF THE CLAIMANT

The Board was sensitive to the cultural differences, however it also notes that the claimant has 15 years of education and was able to articulate very well. We concur with counsel that, for the most part, the claimant was credible. We concur that when he did not know the answer, he did not attempt to speculate.

The claimant traveled to the United States, with the help of a snakehead who procured a U.S. visa on his behalf and his own passport. He testified that he fears the PSB due to his role in assisting his mother in distributing pamphlets to advertise Falun Gong. His mother had commenced Falun Gong activities in XXXX 2009, when she was ill.2 The claimant began distributing materials in XXXX 2010. He was totally aware of the illegality of the activities. However, he believed that, as a non-practitioner, it was less risky for him to carry out this distribution. Nothing untoward occurred between January, 2010 and April, 2011. However, on XXXX XXXX, 2011, he and three others were discovered by the police patrol. He was candid in acknowledging that he was unaware if the police knew of the distribution because he and one other individual were able to escape. The two remaining individuals were arrested. The claimant hid at the home of his cousin, and his mother joined them on the following day. The claimant has no idea what has happened to the two who were arrested.

The claimant testified that on XXXX XXXX, 2011, the PSB came to his home looking for him and his mother. In response to the panel, the claimant acknowledged that he had no idea how the PSB would know he was involved and hence the knowledge of his address. He did, however, speculate that perhaps the two individuals who were arrested were coerced into divulging this information.

On XXXX XXXX, 2011, a summons was issued against the claimant and his mother.3 On XXXX XXXX, 2012, his mother was arrested after returning to her hometown to visit her gravely ill mother. She was arrested during a hospital visit, having returned on XXXX XXXX, 2012. The claimant testified that the PSB had visited their home 5-6 times between XXXX XXXX, 2011 and XXXX XXXX, 2012. Since then, there have been additional visits; according to the claimant, there have been in excess of a total of 10 visits. The claimant was able to provide to the panel the months of these visits.

While, for the most part, the panel found the claimant's testimony to be credible, it seems implausible that the day after her return, while in the hospital, she would be arrested. However, the claimant submitted an arrest warrant issued on XXXX XXXX, 2012. The jail visiting card is only a photocopy, and, therefore, cannot be accorded full weight.

The claimant departed China from the Beijing airport using his own passport. In response to the panel, he indicated that he had shown his passport three times at the airport - check-in, security, and boarding. However, in response to counsel, he added that the snakehead had bribed a security official to allow him to pass through security.

Even if we believe the foregoing, the passport, having been shown on three occasions, would have been scanned. Therefore, we conclude that the officials had the opportunity to detain or interrogate the claimant at more than one location in the airport.

The panel notes the claimant has identified he fears arrest by the PSB in China. His oral testimony alleges the PSB have been pursuing his whereabouts on numerous occasions. The claimant possessed a valid Chinese passport.4 Documentary evidence indicates the Chinese authorities have access to a computerized record system,5 which has the ability to track entry/exit from the country. The panel finds it reasonable to believe that if, as the claimant alleges, the PSB were repeatedly seeking the claimant, the PSB would be aware of his ability to flee the country.
This begs the question as to why he was not questioned at the time of his exit from China.

The panel notes the PSB has a computer linked security system6 that contains information on individuals who would be persons of interest to the PSB. It would be reasonable to believe therefore that the claimant's name and his address would be linked and identified in this system. When reviewing documentary evidence7 on entry and exit procedures as well as the "Golden Shield" system, the panel concludes it is not plausible if the claimant was being sought by the PSB that his passport could be scanned through the computer system at the airport without detection. Given the alleged PSB interest in the claimant, the panel concludes, on a balance of probabilities, it is unlikely that the claimant would have been able to leave China without being detected. The panel acknowledges that the documentation states, in part, that, in some instances, there have been reports of police not sharing information. However, given the alleged pursuit of the claimant by the PSB, it is reasonable to expect that the claimant's name would have been entered in the database as a person wanted by the PSB and, as such, he would not have been able to exit the country.
The claimant's testimony runs counter to documentary evidence about the PSB's methods as well as normal entry/exit procedures and is found to be lacking in credibility.

In reviewing the claimant's testimony in the areas discussed above, the panel concludes, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not being sought for arrest by the authorities in China for his assistance in distributing pamphlets to support his mother's practice of Falun Gong.

Moreover, the panel acknowledges that those who knowingly support the activities of Falun Gong practitioners through the sale and distribution of Falun Gong material are at risk of sanctions because these activities promote the practice of an illegal activity which had been banned by the PRC since July 22, 1999. Representatives of the Falun Dafa Association of Canada note that there have been reports that persons who assist Falun Gong practitioners could face fines, threats and harassment even though they themselves are not practitioners.

The panel notes that the Court of Appeal in Zolfagharkhani8 set forth "some general propositions relating to the status of an ordinary law of general application in determining the question of persecution": (1) The statutory definition of Convention refugee makes the intent (or any principal effect)9 of an ordinary law of general application, rather than the motivation of the claimant, relevant to the existence of persecution.10 (2) But the neutrality of an ordinary law of general application, vis-à-vis the five grounds for refugee status, must be judged objectively by Canadian tribunals and courts when required.11 (3) In such consideration, an ordinary law of general application, even in non-democratic societies, should ... be given a presumption of validity and neutrality, and the onus should be on a claimant, as is generally the case in refugee cases, to show that the laws are either inherently or for some other reason persecutory.12 (4) It will not be enough for the claimant to show that a particular regime is generally oppressive but rather that the law in question is persecutory in relation to a Convention ground.

Based on the evidence tendered by the claimant, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant would be, at most, prosecuted in China for aiding and abetting the activities of his mother. The claimant acknowledged the illegality of his activities and yet he continued over a period of 16 months to assist his mother.

The claimant stated he feared arrest by the PSB. While the panel does not have sufficient credible evidence to agree with the claimant on this point, it has considered an additional analysis based on the assumption that he would be convicted at trial.

The panel has looked at the documentary evidence,13 which clearly highlights that Falun Gong is considered a cult, and the authorities have taken the extraordinary measures to root out the participants and have focused their attention on non-participants who may be seen as aiding practitioners. The establishment of a 610 office in every province, town and county in China as well as in every university, government body and state-owned enterprise highlights the length the authorities have gone to try and identify individual associated with Falun Gong.

The panel acknowledges that those who support the activities of Falun Gong practitioners through the production of Falun Gong material such as the claimant are at risk of sanctions because these activities promote the practice of an illegal activity which has been banned by the People's Republic of China since July 22nd, 1999. Representatives of the Falun Dafa Association note there have been reports that persons who assist Falun Gong practitioners could face fines, threats and harassment even though they themselves are not practitioners.14

Subsection 97(1) of the Act reads as follows: * Persons in Need of Protection 97. (1) A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally o (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or o (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if * (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themselves of the protection of that country, * (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, * (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and * (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care.

The panel finds that, if the claimant returns to China and is convicted at trial, it is inherent or incidental to the lawful sanctions in China. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the panel does acknowledge that lawful sanctions cannot be imposed in disregard for accepted international standards.

The panel has considered section 33(f) of the Act, which directs that the Act be construed and applied in a manner that complies with international human rights instruments to which Canada is a signatory. The test that is used is whether the punishment that the claimant may reasonably face in China would shock the conscience of Canadians.

At the hearing, the claimant indicated that his mother remains in detention, although he has no knowledge of the other two individuals who were arrested in his company. The panel also notes that the evidence of human rights abuses in general in a country is not in itself sufficient to show that the claimant is personally at risk of harm. Chinese laws may be harsher than Canadian laws or the prisons may not be the same standard as Canadian prisons; however, this is not sufficient ground to grant a claim under section 97(1).

Assuming that the claimant would be incarcerated on conviction, the panel has considered what prison conditions the claimant would face. The panel has reviewed the documentary evidence on Chinese prison conditions. The panel notes that, though the conditions in many penal institutions are harsh and degrading, the conditions are generally such that the prisoners' basic needs and rights are accommodated.

The Report of the Special Rapporteur on torture and cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment or punishment published on the 10th of March, 2006 states: The Special Rapporteur visited a total of ten detention facilities. In general, the Special Rapporteur found that although the specific conditions of the facilities varied, in terms of basic conditions, such as food, medicine, and hygiene, they were generally satisfactory. However, the Special Rapporteur noticed a palpable level of fear when talking to detainees. He also was struck by the strict level of discipline exerted on the detainees in different facilities. Time and again, he entered cells and found all detainees sitting cross-legged on a mattress or in a similar forced position reading the criminal law or prison rules. According to information provided by detainees, such forced re-education, in particular in pre-trial detention centres, goes on for most of the day. Even when serving long prison sentences, persons convicted of political offences usually have no right to work and very little time for recreation. They are not allowed to practise their religion.15
On the panel's examination of the gravity of the offence, the legal processes in China, and the proposed method of punishment, the panel does not find that subsection 97(1) applies to the claimant.

As such, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that, if the claimant were to be pursued by authorities in China, it is because he has violated Chinese law and not because he holds a particular belief or that he is in opposition of government policies. I further find, on a balance of probabilities, that the sanctions that could be imposed upon him amounts to fines, threats and harassment and fall short of establishing that he would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and risk of torture. As such, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that he would only be at risk of prosecution rather than persecution should he return to China. I note that prosecution for a violation of country laws is not in itself a United Nations recognized basis for a refugee claim. In any case, I find, on the basis of the cumulative findings and negative inferences I have noted above, that the claimant has failed to satisfy his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

I am supported in this determination by the decision of Madam Justice Dawson. Justice Dawson noted in her decision that the evidence did not support those who sympathize with or associate with Falun Gong practitioners and are arrested and subjected to cruel and unusual punishment. Justice Dawson also notes in her decision that the treatment that those who harbour practitioners may receive is, on the whole, more consistent with harassment or discrimination and falls short of the conduct that is contemplated by sections of 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

Based of the totality of findings noted above, the panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture.

The panel has considered all three protection grounds under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and, on the basis of the totality of all the evidence made available to the panel, finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted in China, nor that he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

For these reasons, the claim is rejected.
